summary: A guide for implementers of software that sends faxes through Internet mail using RFC 2305 and RFC 2532. It does not override those documents. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: This is a tips sheet for people building programs that send a fax by email.

questions: what is simple mode vs extended mode fax
how does fax over email confirm delivery
subtitle: Practical fixes and cautions for anyone building software that sends faxes over Internet mail.

tldr.problem: Internet fax standards (RFC 2305 for Simple Mode, RFC 2532 for Extended Mode, RFC 2301 for the file format) left room for implementations that deviate in ways that break interoperability.
tldr.mechanism: This guide clarifies how senders and receivers should handle multipart/alternative, delivery and disposition notifications, TIFF files, content types and fax addresses.
tldr.outcome: It is informational and does not supersede the documents it refers to; following it helps different fax-by-email products work together.

today: RFC 3249 is an Informational document and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It guides implementers of RFC 2305 and RFC 2532 and does not override them.

sections.title: Purpose and Terminology
sections.content:
This guide clarifies published RFCs that standardize facsimile communications using Internet email. Its intent is to prevent implementations that deviate in a way that causes interoperability problems. It does not supersede the documents it clarifies.

It uses a few shorthand terms. Simple Mode is RFC 2305 and Extended Mode is RFC 2532. MDN is a Message Disposition Notification (RFC 2298) and DSN is a Delivery Status Notification (RFC 1894). TIFF means profile S or F of the fax file format, delivered as image/tiff, while TIFF-FX means other profiles, sent as image/tiff-fx.
sections.plainLanguage: Fax-by-email has rules, but people read them differently. This sheet says how to read them so every machine plays the same game.

sections.title: Simple Mode and multipart/alternative
sections.content:
Some email clients cannot correctly process a message whose content type is multipart/alternative, even though MIME requires it. If a sender is unsure whether the recipient can handle it, the sender should assume the worst and not use that content type.

Receivers with little storage cannot keep earlier parts of such a message. They may simply use the first part they can process, even if a later part has higher fidelity. When two high-fidelity but low-memory devices talk, the lowest-fidelity part is then used.

The fix is for the sender to learn the recipient's capabilities and send only high-fidelity parts. No mechanism exists to learn this before the first message. After that, Extended Mode lets a recipient report its capabilities in a DSN (if it is an ESMTP server) or in an MDN (if it is a user agent). These points also apply to Extended Mode.
sections.plainLanguage: Sending several versions of a picture in one envelope can confuse small machines, which grab the first one they can read, even if it is the blurriest.

sections.title: Extended Mode Confirmations
sections.content:
A sender that wants confirmation should include a Message-ID header with its Disposition-Notification-To header, so MDNs can be matched to the original message. DSNs are best matched using the ENVID parameter in the MAIL command.

The attachment, not the body, is the fax, so receivers are recommended to acknowledge success or failure to decode the attachment. A catch: RFC 2298 does not distinguish decoding the body from decoding an attachment, so an MDN may describe the body only. For a device that prints or forwards the fax, the guide suggests a disposition-type of dispatched on success, and processed with disposition-modifier error on failure, with matching human-readable text.

Because legacy mail programs do not parse machine-readable headers, subjects such as "Your message was processed successfully. (MDN)" or "Your message could not be delivered. (DSN)" help users recognise the outcome.
sections.plainLanguage: When a fax arrives, the receiver should send back a note saying whether it worked, using plain words people can read.

sections.title: SMTP, POP3 and IMAP4 Receivers
sections.content:
SMTP-server receivers are strongly encouraged to implement enhanced error codes (RFC 2034). The RFC gives example sessions. In the success case the server answers 250 2.0.0 Message accepted and a DSN reports Action: delivered. If the decode error is found after acceptance, a failure DSN reports status 5.6.1 (Media not supported). If it is found before acceptance, the server replies 554 5.6.1 Media not supported and the previous MTA generates the DSN.

For POP3 or IMAP4 receivers, the guide shows MDNs using existing values from RFC 2298 and defines no new ones. An MDN with an error or warning modifier suggests the file may not have been decoded, but nothing ties the disposition to the body or to the attachment.

With several attachments, no mechanism says which decoded. A receiver unable to decode any of them is recommended to return a decoding error for the whole message.
sections.plainLanguage: The examples show the exact notes a mail server or mail program should send back, whether the fax worked or not.

sections.title: The TIFF File Format
sections.content:
A TIFF Image File Directory (IFD) must start on a word boundary, and a word should be read as a 2-byte quantity. Because low-memory devices may not cope with arbitrary IFD placement, senders are strongly recommended to place the IFD at the beginning of the file for any profile.

Interoperability testing found problems. Some common writers produced big-endian files although Profile S calls for little-endian, so readers should cope with both while writers always write little-endian. Byte order markers other than II or MM were seen, so readers should tolerate them and writers use the correct value.

The guide also lists many reader and writer rules: be liberal in what readers accept (for example IFDs out of order, or SHORT instead of LONG) and strict in what writers produce (correct tag types, counts, ordering, the magic number 42, a single byte order, and consistent tag values). For L*a*b* color it advises matching the ITULAB gamut to the image source, since the default suits scanned hardcopy but not sRGB data.
sections.plainLanguage: The picture file has a table of contents. Writers should put it in the expected place and spell everything correctly, while readers should be forgiving of small mistakes.

sections.title: Content Types, Addresses and Security
sections.content:
The content type image/tiff should only be used for Profiles S and F. Using it for other profiles is deprecated; image/tiff-fx should be used instead. To work with devices that render only Profile S or F, image/tiff SHOULD be used for those profiles.

The + and = characters are valid in message headers but must be encoded in some ESMTP values, notably ORCPT. For example, FAX=+390408565@example.com in a header becomes FAX+3D+2B390408565@example.com in ORCPT.

For security, the RFC points to Section 5 of RFC 2305 and Section 4 of RFC 2532.
sections.plainLanguage: Some characters need a disguise when passed to a mail server, and each kind of picture file should carry the right label.
